# True or false: Leaders

For CTOs, CIOs, architects and executives: decisions, crises, boards and portfolios. Test the beliefs that shape how technology is led.

10 statements (Foundation 3, Standard 7). Decide whether each one is true or false before you open the answer. Every answer says why and links to the page that teaches it.

Prefer the terminal? From the repository root, run `python3 exercises/quiz.py --area leaders`.

### 1. Most decisions are reversible 'two-way doors' and should be made quickly by an individual or a small group.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Jeff Bezos's 2015 Amazon shareholder letter separates Type 1 decisions, which are hard to reverse, from Type 2 decisions, which can be undone. Most decisions are Type 2. Giving them the heavy process meant for one-way doors makes an organisation slow.

Read more: [leaders/decision-making.md](../../leaders/decision-making.md)

</details>

### 2. A pre-mortem asks the team to imagine that the project has already failed and to explain why.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Gary Klein described the method in Harvard Business Review in 2007. Treating the failure as a fact makes doubt a task instead of disloyalty, so people raise concerns they would otherwise keep quiet. Run it for heavy, hard-to-reverse decisions, while the plan can still change.

Read more: [leaders/decision-making.md](../../leaders/decision-making.md)

</details>

### 3. Paying the ransom is the quickest safe way to recover from a ransomware attack.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** The UK NCSC and US CISA advise against paying, and paying does not guarantee that data will be decrypted or that stolen data will be deleted. Facilitating a payment can also breach sanctions rules, as the 2021 US Treasury OFAC advisory warns, so take legal advice. Recovery usually depends on immutable backups restored into a clean environment.

Read more: [leaders/crisis-leadership.md](../../leaders/crisis-leadership.md)

</details>

### 4. In a complex situation, the Cynefin framework suggests running small, safe experiments before committing to a course.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Snowden and Boone (Harvard Business Review, 2007) describe complex situations as ones where cause and effect are clear only in hindsight. There, leaders probe, sense and respond rather than apply a known best practice. A common failure is commissioning a long analysis when only an experiment will tell you the answer.

Read more: [leaders/decision-making.md](../../leaders/decision-making.md)

</details>

### 5. A new CTO should announce major changes in the first week to show decisive leadership.

Level: Foundation

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** New leaders fail more often from acting on a diagnosis they have not checked than from moving too slowly. Spend the first 30 days listening and measuring, and change little in the first month except what is unsafe. Reorganise only after the strategy is written.

Read more: [leaders/first-90-days.md](../../leaders/first-90-days.md)

</details>

### 6. OKR key results should be a list of tasks the team will complete.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** A key result is a number with a baseline, a target and a data source, and it measures an outcome: a change in what users or systems do. A finished task list can leave the objective untouched. Andy Grove described the method in High Output Management (1983).

Read more: [leaders/strategy-toolkit.md](../../leaders/strategy-toolkit.md)

</details>

### 7. Gartner's TIME model sorts applications into Tolerate, Invest, Migrate and Eliminate.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** TIME scores each application on business value and technical fit, then gives it one of four decisions. Invest in high value and good fit; eliminate low value and poor fit on a date, with an owner. Use it when run cost rises every year or nobody can list every application.

Read more: [leaders/strategy-toolkit.md](../../leaders/strategy-toolkit.md)

</details>

### 8. A rehearsal finds gaps in an executive crisis plan that reading the written plan does not.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** The first time executives meet a crisis should not be the real one. An exercise shows who decides, who speaks to customers and regulators, and what is missing; the playbook suggests two a year. Track the findings like postmortem actions and report them to the board.

Read more: [leaders/crisis-leadership.md](../../leaders/crisis-leadership.md)

</details>

### 9. A Wardley map places the parts of a service on a scale from novel to commodity, which helps decide what to build and what to buy.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**True.** Simon Wardley's maps show the components a user need depends on and how far each has evolved, from genesis to commodity. Novel parts may be worth building. Parts that have moved to product or commodity are candidates to buy or adopt, and building a commodity in-house is a common, expensive mistake.

Read more: [leaders/strategy-toolkit.md](../../leaders/strategy-toolkit.md)

</details>

### 10. Cyber security is a technical matter that a board can safely leave to the IT department.

Level: Standard

<details><summary>Answer</summary>

**False.** Boards and audit committees are accountable for technology risk, including cyber risk. The UK NCSC Board Toolkit is written for board members, with questions to ask on topics such as risk management, suppliers and incident response. The board sets the risk appetite and checks it with a few measures each quarter.

Read more: [leaders/board-and-executive-reporting.md](../../leaders/board-and-executive-reporting.md)

</details>
